subject: Communication
title: Manufacturing Consent: Chomsky's Media Model
description: A quick, practical guide to Manufacturing Consent: Chomsky's Media Model.

hook.text: Noam Chomsky argued that 'free press' in democracies still produces propaganda — just through economics, not censorship.

buildup.text: The propaganda model has five filters: ownership, advertising, sourcing, flak (pushback), and ideology.

discovery.text: When six corporations own 90% of media, their business interests shape what stories get told — and which don't.

twist.text: Critics say Chomsky oversimplifies: journalists do push back, independent media exists, and audiences aren't passive.

climax.text: The model's core insight endures: follow the money. Who pays for media shapes what it produces, in any political system.

punchline.text: Free press doesn't mean free from influence. Follow the money.

quiz.question: How many filters does Chomsky's propaganda model identify?

details.summary: Noam Chomsky and Edward Herman's propaganda model argues that mainstream media filters news through five lenses: ownership, advertising, sourcing, flak, and ideology. These filters systematically favor powerful interests without requiring any conscious conspiracy among journalists.
details.whyItMatters: The propaganda model reveals how structural forces shape news coverage, helping you understand why certain stories dominate while others are ignored.
takeaways: Five filters: ownership, advertising, sourcing, flak, ideology
Structural forces shape news without conscious conspiracy
Corporate ownership concentrates media power in few hands

faq.question: Is the propaganda model a conspiracy theory?
faq.answer: No. Chomsky explicitly argues against conspiracy. The model describes structural incentives that produce predictable outcomes without coordination. Journalists do not conspire; they operate within systems where ownership, advertisers, and sources naturally constrain what gets published.

faq.question: Is the propaganda model still relevant in the internet age?
faq.answer: Partly. While the internet democratized publishing, major platforms still concentrate power. Social media algorithms create new filters. The five original filters still apply to mainstream outlets, and new digital filters like algorithmic curation have been added to the landscape.
